why: Both moved identical traffic with identical code and were honest about embeddings staying off Router, so the decision rests on the system work: A exercised every Router lever that applies to this app (per-role labels, per-conversation cache key worth a measured -49%, provider timeout inside the client's own deadline, a scoped fallback, a cheaper model for synthesis, and the Flex pin broken out as an explicit business choice), ranked them, measured each live on this app's prompts, and reported two measured rejections plus the dominant cost centre as a needs-decision. B contributes two genuinely better pieces of reasoning — end-to-end tokens-per-turn as the only honest way to judge a model swap, and the fact that output tokens and per-document fan-out are half the bill and are app-level, not Router-level — but it ships only two levers, settles for a deployment-wide cache key it knows is the wrong scope, and premises its biggest rework on a constraint A disproved by setting prompt_cache_key through additional_kwargs on the existing client.
A_best: The per-conversation prompt cache key: right scope (not one pool for all tenants), achieved on the existing Chat Completions client with no rework, and proven with a zero-versus-13,824-cached-token A/B through the real Router — the one lever B deferred to an invasive Responses port it did not need.
B_best: Measuring the cheap-model swap end to end rather than per token, and showing it is a trap on this workload (+7% and +219% per turn because output length and agent rounds grow faster than price falls), then naming the real remaining money — 52% of a turn is output tokens over a 13-call, per-document fan-out that Router cannot touch.
A_worst: The sec-chat fallback is asserted to cost nothing while gpt-4o-mini serves, but A never tested healthy-traffic distribution; B measured 4 of 10 healthy calls going to a different vendor at +39%, so A may have put a different model in front of users without knowing it. The gpt-6-luna case also rests on a single 803-token prompt.
B_worst: Thin build-out of Router itself — two items, a cache key at the wrong granularity, and the per-conversation key plus per-request metadata parked behind a protocol-risky Responses/agent migration that A showed is unnecessary; the app-level cost insight in n2 stays a note rather than a ranked, specific proposal.
